title: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
summary: How RFdiffusion and friends generate protein backbones by diffusing rigid residue frames, then get sequences from ProteinMPNN and validate with AlphaFold2 self-consistency.
outcomes: Explain what a residue frame is and compute one from N, CA and C by Gram-Schmidt
Explain why translations get Gaussian noise while rotations need IGSO(3) on SO(3)
Compute an scRMSD by Kabsch alignment and apply the 2 Angstrom designability criterion
Trace the generate-then-design-then-validate funnel and predict where designs are lost
State what RFdiffusion achieved experimentally and where the approach still fails

lessons.title: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem

blocks.md: A **protein** is a chain. Each link in the chain is a **residue**, and every residue contributes the same three main-chain atoms in the same order: a nitrogen (**N**), a central carbon called **CA** (alpha carbon), and a second carbon (**C**) that carries a double-bonded oxygen (**O**). Those four atoms per residue form the **backbone**. Residue i is joined to residue i+1 by a **peptide bond** between the C of one and the N of the next.

What varies between residues is the **side chain**, the group hanging off CA. Nature uses 20 standard amino acids, so a protein of length 100 is one choice out of 20 options at each of 100 positions. The Nobel press release for the 2024 Chemistry prize puts it plainly: proteins generally consist of 20 different amino acids, described as life's building blocks.

Two separate objects, and you must keep them apart:

- **sequence**: which of the 20 amino acids sits at each position (discrete, one symbol per residue)
- **backbone**: where the N, CA, C and O atoms of every residue sit in 3D space (continuous coordinates)

The chain folds into one preferred backbone shape, and that shape is what gives the protein its function.

blocks.title: Three residues of backbone, atom by atom

scenes.caption: Residue 1 contributes N, CA, C and O. Every residue in every protein contributes exactly these four main-chain atoms, in this order.
The C of residue 1 is bonded to the N of residue 2: the peptide bond. The chain is covalently continuous, so the residues cannot move independently.
Each residue's side chain (R1, R2, R3) is one of 20 chemical groups attached at CA. Choosing the side chains is choosing the sequence.
The three CA atoms are the positions a generator will place first. In a real protein consecutive CA atoms sit about 3.8 Angstrom apart.

blocks.md: **Structure prediction** goes from sequence to shape. AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., Nature 2021) solved that direction well enough to matter: at CASP14 its median backbone accuracy over 87 domains was 0.96 Angstrom CA r.m.s.d.95, that is root mean square deviation of CA positions over the best-matching 95 percent of residues, against 2.8 Angstrom for the next best method. **Design** is the opposite direction: you want a shape (or just a function) and must find a chain that folds into it.

Modern design splits that inverse problem in two:

1. **Generate a backbone.** Place the N, CA, C of every residue in 3D, with no sequence at all. This is a continuous geometry problem, which is exactly where diffusion and flow models are strong.
2. **Design a sequence for it.** Given fixed backbone coordinates, pick amino acids that would actually fold that way. This is a discrete 20-way choice per position, done by a separate network (ProteinMPNN).

Splitting this way works because the map from sequence to structure is many-to-one: many different sequences fold to nearly the same backbone, so step 2 has room to search, and you can sample many candidate sequences per backbone and keep the best.

blocks.title: Prediction and design run in opposite directions

scenes.caption: Prediction, the direction AlphaFold2 made routine: a known sequence goes in, a structure comes out.
Design starts from a goal, not a sequence. A generative model places a backbone with no amino acids assigned at all.
A second network reads the fixed backbone and writes a sequence for it. The sequence is then fed back to AlphaFold2 to check that it really folds to the requested shape.

blocks.prompt: Why not run diffusion directly on the sequence of 20 amino acids and skip backbones entirely?
blocks.reveal: Because the thing you want to control is geometry. A design goal like "present these three side chains in this exact arrangement to grip a target" is a statement about 3D coordinates, and coordinates are continuous, so Gaussian noise and a learned denoiser apply directly. A sequence is discrete, and the quantity you care about (the fold) is only revealed after an expensive folding step. Generating geometry first also lets you hand the same backbone to a sequence designer many times and keep whichever attempt validates.

blocks.md: The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised both halves of this picture: one half to David Baker for computational protein design, the other half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction. The two halves are not independent. Design pipelines use a structure predictor as their in silico referee, which is why the rest of this course keeps coming back to AlphaFold2.

blocks.question: You are given a backbone with 120 residues and no sequence. How many continuous coordinates and how many discrete choices does the two-stage pipeline deal with?
options: 120 discrete choices only; the backbone is discrete too
About 1440 coordinates for the backbone (4 atoms x 3 numbers x 120) and 120 choices out of 20 for the sequence
120 coordinates and 120 choices, one of each per residue
20 coordinates per residue and 4 choices per residue
blocks.explain: Each of the 120 residues contributes four backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O), each with 3 coordinates, so roughly 1440 continuous numbers. The sequence is a separate object: one choice among 20 amino acids at each of the 120 positions.

blocks.question: Why does the many-to-one map from sequence to structure help a design pipeline?
options: It means each backbone has exactly one correct sequence, so the search is easy
It means structure prediction is impossible, so designs must be tested in the lab
It means many sequences fold to nearly the same backbone, so you can sample several per backbone and keep the ones that validate
It means the backbone can be ignored once the sequence is chosen
blocks.explain: Many sequences map to nearly the same fold. That redundancy is what makes sampling 8 (or 100) sequences per backbone and filtering them a sensible strategy, rather than needing to find the one true sequence.

lessons.title: A residue is a rigid frame: rotation plus translation

blocks.md: Storing a backbone as raw atom coordinates wastes most of its structure. Bond lengths and bond angles inside one residue barely change: the N to CA distance is about 1.46 Angstrom and the CA to C distance about 1.52 Angstrom in every residue of every protein. The N, CA, C triangle of a residue is effectively **rigid**. What differs between residues is only where that rigid triangle sits and which way it points.

So represent each residue by a **frame**: a translation and a rotation. The translation $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the CA position. The rotation $R \in SO(3)$ is a 3 by 3 matrix with orthonormal columns and determinant +1 that says how the residue's local axes are oriented in the global coordinate system. A frame maps the residue's fixed local atom positions to real-world positions.

blocks.tex: T \cdot a = R\,a + x, \qquad R \in SO(3), \; x \in \mathbb{R}^3
blocks.caption: A frame T is an element of SE(3), the group of rigid motions. A backbone of N residues is N frames, a point in SE(3) to the power N. RFdiffusion and FrameDiff both diffuse exactly this object.

blocks.md: How do you get $R$ from the three atoms? With **Gram-Schmidt**, the standard recipe for turning two independent vectors into an orthonormal basis. Take the two bond vectors out of CA, make the first one a unit vector, remove its component from the second, normalise what is left, and get the third axis as a cross product. Below is the computation on one real set of coordinates (residue 2 of a toy 3-residue backbone, CA atoms at (0.00, 0.00, 0.00), (3.80, 0.00, 0.00) and (5.70, 3.29, 0.00)).

blocks.title: Building one residue frame by Gram-Schmidt
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

N  = np.array([4.78, -0.19, 1.07])   # backbone N of residue 2
CA = np.array([3.80,  0.00, 0.00])   # alpha carbon
C  = np.array([3.25,  1.42, 0.00])   # backbone C

v1 = C - CA                 # CA to C bond vector
v2 = N - CA                 # CA to N bond vector

e1 = v1 / np.linalg.norm(v1)        # first axis
p  = v2 @ e1                        # part of v2 along e1
u  = v2 - p * e1                    # remove it
e2 = u / np.linalg.norm(u)          # second axis
e3 = np.cross(e1, e2)               # third axis

R = np.stack([e1, e2, e3], axis=1)  # rotation of the frame
x = CA                              # translation of the frame

scenes.caption: The two bond vectors out of CA. Their lengths are 1.523 and 1.463 Angstrom and the angle between them is 111.3 degrees, so they are independent but not orthogonal.
Normalise v1 to get the first axis e1. This fixes one direction of the local coordinate system.
Project v2 onto e1 and subtract. The leftover u is perpendicular to e1 by construction, which is the whole trick of Gram-Schmidt.
Normalise u to get e2, then take the cross product for e3. Three mutually orthogonal unit vectors.
Stack the axes as columns: R is orthonormal with det(R) = 1.0, a genuine rotation. Together with x = CA the residue's pose is 6 numbers of freedom, not 12 coordinates.
scenes.output: frame of residue 2: rotation angle 151.5 degrees about its axis, translation (3.80, 0.00, 0.00)

blocks.title: The rotation matrix of residue 2, column by column

scenes.caption: Column e1 is the CA to C direction expressed in global coordinates. Reading a column tells you where a local axis points.
Column e2 is the in-plane direction towards N, after the e1 component was removed.
Column e3 is the normal of the N, CA, C plane. Its sign is fixed by the cross product order, which is why every model must agree on one convention.
All three columns together: each has unit length and any two are orthogonal, so R preserves distances and angles. Nine stored numbers, three degrees of freedom.

blocks.md:
Why bother? Three reasons.

- **Correct degrees of freedom.** Six numbers per residue instead of twelve, and bond lengths can never come out wrong because they live in the fixed local geometry.
- **A place to put noise.** Translations live in $\mathbb{R}^3$, where Gaussian noise is natural. Rotations live on the curved manifold $SO(3)$, which needs its own noise process (next lesson).
- **Equivariance.** If you rotate and translate the whole protein, every frame transforms the same way, so a network built on frames can be made to respect that symmetry instead of learning it from data.

FrameDiff (Yim et al., 2023) makes this explicit: it builds a diffusion on SE(3) to the power N whose metric is the sum of the SO(3) and the $\mathbb{R}^3$ metrics, so the two parts can be noised independently.

A frame is not a whole residue. The side chain is missing entirely, and even the backbone O is placed afterwards from a torsion angle. A generated backbone is a scaffold, not a protein: it has no chemistry until a sequence is designed for it.

blocks.question: You rotate an entire generated protein by 90 degrees about the z axis. What happens to the frames?
options: Every frame's rotation is left-multiplied by the same rotation and every translation is rotated; the protein is unchanged in substance
Only the translations change; the rotations are stored in local coordinates and are unaffected
Only the rotations change; CA positions are absolute and never move
The frames become invalid because the columns of R are no longer orthonormal
blocks.explain: A global rigid motion acts on every frame identically: each R becomes (global R) times R and each x becomes (global R) x plus the translation. The protein itself is the same object, which is exactly the symmetry an SE(3) model is built to respect.

blocks.question: Gram-Schmidt subtracts the e1 component from the CA to N vector before normalising. What would go wrong if you skipped the subtraction and just normalised both bond vectors?
options: The matrix would still be a rotation, since both vectors have unit length
The determinant would be negative instead of positive
The third axis would be undefined because the cross product of unit vectors is zero
The two columns would not be orthogonal (the bond angle is 111.3 degrees, not 90), so R would not be in SO(3) and would distort distances
blocks.explain: Unit length is not enough: a rotation matrix needs orthogonal columns. The N-CA-C angle is about 111 degrees, so the two normalised bond vectors are not perpendicular, and a matrix built from them would stretch and shear instead of rotate.

lessons.title: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations

blocks.md: Recall the one idea from the prereq course: a forward process destroys data into a simple distribution, and a network learns to run time backwards, either as a score or as a velocity field. Here the data point is not an image. It is a list of N frames, so the forward process has to corrupt translations and rotations at the same time, and each needs its own kind of noise.

**Translations are easy.** They live in $\mathbb{R}^3$, so use the usual variance-preserving process $dx = -\tfrac{1}{2} x \, dt + dB$ whose marginal at time t is a scaled sample plus Gaussian noise. One subtlety: no probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^3$ is invariant to global translation, so FrameDiff removes the centre of mass of the translations, and diffuses the centred coordinates. Without that, the model would have to learn that a protein shifted by 100 Angstrom is the same protein.

blocks.tex: x^{(t)} = e^{-t/2} x^{(0)} + \sqrt{1 - e^{-t}}\; z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_3)
blocks.caption: At t = 0.1 the data is scaled by 0.951 and noise std is 0.308; at t = 1.0 the scale is 0.607 and the noise std is 0.795. Translations in Angstrom, so by t = 1 the noise is comparable to a bond length.

blocks.md: Below are the three CA atoms of the toy backbone, noised with one fixed draw of standard normals at two noise scales. Watch the CA to CA distances, which should stay near 3.80 Angstrom in any real protein.

blocks.title: The same Gaussian draw at two noise scales

scenes.caption: The clean backbone: three CA atoms, consecutive ones 3.80 Angstrom apart, which is what a trans peptide bond enforces.
One fixed draw of three standard normal vectors, one per residue. These same numbers are reused at both noise scales so the comparison is apples to apples.
Noise scale 1.0 Angstrom. The chain is still recognisable but residue 3 has drifted: the second CA-CA distance is 5.79 Angstrom, chemically impossible. Local geometry breaks first.
Noise scale 5.0 Angstrom. Distances of 4.41 and 14.35 Angstrom: the chain is gone and only a cloud of points is left. This is the regime the reverse process starts from.

blocks.md: **Rotations are the interesting half.** You cannot add a Gaussian to a rotation matrix: the result is not orthonormal. Instead run Brownian motion on the manifold $SO(3)$ itself. Its transition density has a name, **IGSO(3)** (isotropic Gaussian on SO(3)), and it depends only on the rotation angle $\omega$ between the start and the end rotation. FrameDiff gives it as a heat-kernel series, and truncates the sum numerically.

blocks.caption: The density of the angle itself is this f times the uniform (Haar) angle density $(1 - \cos\omega)/\pi$. Summing 3000 terms, the mean rotation angle is 20.4 degrees at t = 0.05, 40.5 at t = 0.2, 87.2 at t = 1.0 and 124.5 at t = 4.0.

blocks.md:
Two limits make IGSO(3) intuitive, and both are visible in the figure below.

- **Small t**: the rotation barely moves, so the manifold looks flat near the start and IGSO(3) is close to an isotropic Gaussian in the axis-angle tangent space. The angle then follows a Maxwell density with scale about $\sqrt{t}$. Numerically the two densities differ by an L1 distance of only 0.015 at t = 0.2.
- **Large t**: all orientation information is gone and IGSO(3) approaches the uniform distribution on $SO(3)$, whose angle density is $(1 - \cos\omega)/\pi$ with mean angle 126.5 degrees. At t = 4.0 the L1 distance to uniform is already 0.045.

blocks.title: How the rotation angle spreads out as noise grows

scenes.caption: s = 0.45, about t = 0.2. Orientations have drifted by a mean of 40.5 degrees: the structure is perturbed but its fold is still readable.
s = 1.0, about t = 1.0. Mean angle 87.2 degrees. The Maxwell approximation is starting to leave the valid angle range, which is why the exact series is needed here.

s = 2.0, about t = 4.0. The exact IGSO(3) density has flattened onto the uniform curve, mean angle 124.5 against the uniform limit of 126.5, but the plotted Maxwell stand-in has broken down: only 52 percent of its mass is still below pi.

blocks.prompt: The reverse process has to undo both noises. Which do you think is harder for the network to get right at low noise: the translations or the rotations?
blocks.reveal: Rotations, and the figure above says why. At small t the translations have moved by a fraction of an Angstrom, but a mean orientation drift of 40 degrees already scrambles which way each residue's side chain would point, and side-chain packing is what makes a fold real. This is also why the loss matters: RFdiffusion trains with a plain mean squared error between predicted and true frames, with no alignment, rather than the alignment-invariant FAPE loss used for structure prediction, precisely so that the predicted global frame stays consistent from one timestep to the next.

blocks.md: **The denoiser.** RFdiffusion (Watson et al., Nature 2023) does not train a network from scratch. It takes the pretrained RoseTTAFold structure prediction network, changes it minimally so its main input is the noised frames rather than a sequence, and fine-tunes it to predict the denoised structure. Fine-tuning from pretrained weights worked far better than training the same architecture from scratch for the same time. Training noises real PDB structures for up to 200 steps, and generation typically runs 200 steps (the paper reports that far fewer, around 15, can suffice for 100-residue designs).

scenes.caption: Sampling starts from random frames: translations from a Gaussian, rotations uniform on SO(3).
The network predicts the fully denoised structure in one shot. The sampler does not keep that prediction; it takes a partial step towards it and re-noises to the next lower timestep.

Self-conditioning: the previous x0 prediction is fed back as a template input, an idea taken from AlphaFold2 recycling. RFdiffusion reports that it substantially improved in silico benchmark performance.
After the last step the x0 prediction is the backbone. It still has no sequence: that is the next lesson.

blocks.md:
Two closely related models are worth knowing, because they isolate what is doing the work.

- **FrameDiff** (Yim et al., 2023) learns the SE(3) score from scratch, with no pretrained structure predictor, and still generates designable backbones up to 500 amino acids. So the frame diffusion formulation itself carries much of the load.
- **FrameFlow** (Yim et al., 2023) replaces the diffusion with flow matching on SE(3): the same frames, a learned vector field instead of a score. It reports about five times fewer sampling steps and roughly twofold better designability than FrameDiff.
- **Chroma** (Ingraham et al., Nature 2023) chooses a different forward process: correlated noise that respects polymer statistics, so noised structures look like collapsed random polymers with chain and radius-of-gyration constraints rather than independent point clouds.

blocks.question: Why does the rotation part of the forward process use IGSO(3) instead of adding Gaussian noise to the nine entries of R?
options: IGSO(3) is faster to sample than a Gaussian
Because a Gaussian perturbation of the nine entries leaves a matrix that is not orthonormal, so it is not a rotation at all
Because rotations have nine degrees of freedom and Gaussians only model three
Because the loss must be invariant to global rotation
blocks.explain: SO(3) is a curved manifold embedded in 9-dimensional space. Adding independent Gaussian noise to the entries leaves the manifold: columns stop being orthonormal and the determinant stops being 1. IGSO(3) is the transition density of Brownian motion that stays on the manifold.

blocks.question: At the start of sampling, what is the distribution of a residue's orientation?
options: The orientation of the nearest residue in the training set
Close to uniform on SO(3): all orientations equally likely, mean pairwise angle about 126.5 degrees
Identity, because the noise schedule starts from the identity rotation
A Maxwell density with scale 0.45 radians
blocks.explain: The large-t limit of IGSO(3) is the uniform (Haar) measure on SO(3). The computed mean angle at t = 4.0 is 124.5 degrees, already within 2 degrees of the uniform limit of 126.5, and the L1 distance between the two densities is 0.045.

lessons.title: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check

blocks.md: A backbone is a hypothesis. To test it you need a sequence, and for that the standard tool is **ProteinMPNN** (Dauparas et al., Science 2022). It is a message passing graph network over the residues, with 3 encoder and 3 decoder layers and 128 hidden dimensions, whose input features are distances between the backbone N, CA, C, O atoms and a virtual CB (the first side-chain carbon, placed from the backbone atoms). It writes the sequence autoregressively, but the decoding order is sampled randomly from all permutations rather than fixed left to right, so any subset of positions can be fixed and the rest filled in.

The headline number: on a test set of 402 monomer backbones, ProteinMPNN recovered 52.4 percent of the native sequence, against 32.9 percent for the physics-based Rosetta protocol. Median recovery was 52 percent for monomers, 55 percent for homomers and 51 percent for heteromers. Experimentally, redesigning previously insoluble AlphaFold-hallucinated designs turned 73 of 96 into soluble proteins, with median yield 247 mg per litre against 9 mg per litre for the originals.

Sequence recovery is a proxy, not a goal. A design that recovers 100 percent of a natural sequence has designed nothing new, and a design that recovers 30 percent may fold perfectly well. Recovery is useful only because it correlates with getting the physics right. What you actually test is whether the designed sequence folds back to the backbone you asked for.

That test is **self-consistency**. Take the designed sequence, predict its structure with AlphaFold2 (RFdiffusion runs AF2 on the single sequence, with no multiple sequence alignment, so the prediction cannot lean on homologues) and measure how far the prediction is from the backbone you generated. The distance measure is **RMSD** over CA atoms, and because two structures can be placed anywhere in space, the comparison must minimise over rigid motions.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{scRMSD} = \min_{R \in SO(3),\, x \in \mathbb{R}^3} \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert R p_i + x - q_i \rVert^2}
blocks.caption: p are the designed CA coordinates, q the predicted ones. The minimum has a closed form, found by the Kabsch procedure: centre both sets, take a singular value decomposition (SVD, a factoring into a rotation, a scaling and a rotation) of the cross-covariance, and fix the sign of the determinant.

blocks.title: Kabsch alignment and scRMSD, step by step
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

# 4 CA atoms of a designed backbone, and the AF2
# prediction of the sequence designed for it
P = np.array([[0.00, 0.00, 0.00], [3.80, 0.00, 0.00],
              [5.70, 3.29, 0.00], [8.90, 5.35, 0.00]])
Q = np.array([[1.47,  4.74,  0.52], [2.43,  8.39, -0.63],
              [1.04, 11.31,  0.68], [0.98, 15.74,  1.02]])

cP, cQ = P.mean(0), Q.mean(0)      # centroids
X, Y = P - cP, Q - cQ              # centre both sets

H = X.T @ Y                        # 3x3 cross-covariance
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H)
d = np.sign(np.linalg.det(Vt.T @ U.T))
R = Vt.T @ np.diag([1, 1, d]) @ U.T

dev = X @ R.T - Y                  # residuals after alignment
rmsd = np.sqrt((dev ** 2).sum() / len(P))

scenes.caption: Compare the raw coordinate lists and you get 9.431 Angstrom, which says nothing: the prediction is simply sitting somewhere else in space.
scenes.output: raw per-atom distance is dominated by the arbitrary placement of the prediction

scenes.caption: Subtract the centroids. This removes the translation exactly: the optimal x is always the one that matches the two centres of mass.

Build the 3 by 3 cross-covariance H and take its SVD. The designed backbone is exactly flat (every z is 0), which is why the third singular value is exactly 0, and the first singular value dominates the other two.
The determinant sign guards against a reflection. Here d = +1, so no correction is needed; if it were negative, the last singular direction is flipped to keep R a rotation rather than a mirror.

Rotate and measure. Per-atom deviations of 0.258, 0.156, 0.266 and 0.417 Angstrom give a squared-deviation sum of 0.336 and scRMSD = 0.29 Angstrom. The same two structures that looked 9.4 apart agree to a third of an Angstrom.
scenes.output: scRMSD = 0.29 Angstrom, comfortably under the 2 Angstrom designability cutoff

blocks.md: Any structural comparison in this field is after optimal superposition. A reported RMSD of 1.4 Angstrom always means 1.4 after Kabsch alignment; the unaligned number is meaningless because it depends on where the coordinates happen to be written down.

Now do that for every sequence of a backbone. The figure below takes one toy 8-residue backbone, generates 8 perturbed stand-ins for AF2 predictions with growing error, and computes scRMSD for each with the procedure above. This is a simplified model of the real spread: real predictions are not random perturbations, but the shape of the outcome, a few good sequences and several bad ones, is what the real pipeline sees.

blocks.title: scRMSD of 8 designed sequences for one backbone

scenes.caption: Eight sequences, eight structure predictions, eight scRMSD values computed by Kabsch alignment: 0.33, 0.48, 0.93, 1.32, 2.25, 3.65, 4.01 and 4.78 Angstrom.
Apply the designability cutoff of 2 Angstrom. Four of the eight sequences pass and four do not, which is normal; this is why a single sequence per backbone is a weak test.
The backbone is scored by its best sequence, 0.33 Angstrom here, so this backbone counts as designable. The other seven results are discarded.

blocks.md:
The actual thresholds used in the literature:

- **FrameDiff** and most follow-up work call a backbone designable if $\mathrm{scRMSD} < 2$ Angstrom, and say so explicitly as a stricter filter than the scTM > 0.5 criterion Chroma used, where scTM is the same self-consistency comparison scored by TM-score (a 0 to 1 fold-similarity score) instead of RMSD.
- **RFdiffusion** counts a design as an in silico success when AF2, run from a single sequence, has mean predicted aligned error below 5, lies within 2 Angstrom backbone RMSD of the design, and within 1 Angstrom on any scaffolded functional site. For oligomers the extended data uses mean **pLDDT** above 80, where pLDDT is AF2's predicted local distance difference test: a per-residue self-estimate of accuracy on the lDDT scale, which tracks true accuracy closely (the AlphaFold2 paper fits lDDT-CA = 0.997 pLDDT minus 1.17).
- RFdiffusion typically designs **eight ProteinMPNN sequences per backbone** and scores the backbone by the best of them.

Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

blocks.question: A design has scRMSD of 0.29 Angstrom and mean pLDDT of 42. What is the sensible reading?
options: Designable and high confidence: low RMSD plus any pLDDT is enough
The pLDDT is irrelevant once scRMSD is below 2 Angstrom
Contradictory: the prediction matches the target shape but the predictor says it does not trust its own answer, so the design should not be trusted either
The scRMSD must have been computed without alignment
blocks.explain: The two numbers measure different things. scRMSD says the predicted shape matches the requested shape; pLDDT says how much AF2 trusts that prediction. A low-confidence prediction that happens to match is weak evidence, which is why pipelines filter on confidence (mean pLDDT above 80 for oligomers, mean pAE below 5) as well as on RMSD.

blocks.question: Why does RFdiffusion run AlphaFold2 on the single designed sequence, with no multiple sequence alignment?
options: A designed sequence has no natural homologues, so an MSA would either be empty or misleading; single-sequence prediction is also the harder, more honest test
Because AF2 is faster without an MSA and the pipeline needs throughput
Because MSAs are only used for membrane proteins
Because the sequence is already known to be correct, so extra evidence would bias the result
blocks.explain: A de novo design is not a member of any natural protein family, so there is nothing meaningful to align it to. Running single-sequence prediction also means the model must fold the design from its own learned physics, which is a stricter test than letting it copy a homologue.

lessons.title: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works

blocks.md: Put the pieces together and a protein design campaign is a funnel. Each stage is cheap relative to the next, so the point of each filter is to avoid paying for the one after it. The counts below are illustrative, chosen to match published rates, not measurements from a single run.

blocks.title: The design funnel with illustrative counts

scenes.caption: Stage 1: 200 steps of frame diffusion per backbone, repeated 100 times. Pure GPU time, no lab cost.
Stage 2: eight ProteinMPNN sequences per backbone. Sequence design is cheap, so you take many shots per scaffold.
Stage 3: one AlphaFold2 prediction per sequence, 800 in total. This is the expensive in silico step and it is still far cheaper than ordering genes.

Stage 4: score each backbone by its best sequence and keep those under 2 Angstrom scRMSD. At FrameDiff's 28 percent designability, which it measured with ESMFold rather than AF2, that leaves 28 of 100 backbones.
Stage 5: only the survivors become DNA, protein and assays. RFdiffusion tested on the order of 95 designs per target across five targets and found binders for all five.

blocks.md: Why eight sequences and not one? Suppose a single sequence passes the 2 Angstrom filter with probability p, independently. Then a backbone passes if any of its M sequences does, with probability $1 - (1-p)^M$. Calibrating so that M = 8 gives FrameDiff's reported 28 percent needs p = 0.040: a single sequence would pass only 4 percent of the time. Best-of-8 is a sevenfold improvement for eight times the (cheap) prediction cost.

scenes.caption: With p = 0.040 the independent model reproduces the measured 28 percent at M = 8 by construction, and predicts 15 percent at M = 4 and 48 percent at M = 16.

The model then predicts 98 percent at M = 100. FrameDiff measured 40 percent. The gap is the whole lesson: the eight sequences for one backbone are highly correlated, so a backbone that is geometrically bad stays bad no matter how many sequences you try.
Raising p to 0.10 (a better generator, not more sampling) lifts the M = 8 curve to 57 percent. Improving the backbone generator beats increasing M once M is past a handful.

blocks.md: More sampling buys you less than independence suggests. Sequence sampling cannot rescue an undesignable backbone, which is why designability of the generator, measured at a fixed small M, is the metric the backbone papers compete on.

What came out of the lab, from the RFdiffusion paper:

- **Binder design.** Conditioning on hotspot residues of a target, overall 19 percent of designs bound at or above half the positive control's maximal response, with on the order of 95 designs tested per target and binders found for all five targets. The best anti-HA and anti-IL-7Ra binders had affinities around 30 nM. The authors describe this as roughly two orders of magnitude better than their previous Rosetta-based pipeline.
- **Motif scaffolding.** Given functional site coordinates to build around, RFdiffusion solved 23 of 25 benchmark problems, against 15 for hallucination and 19 for RFjoint inpainting.
- **Fold conditioning.** In silico success rates of 42.5 percent for TIM barrels and 54.1 percent for NTF2 folds.
- **Metal-binding assemblies.** Of 36 designs tested by calorimetry, 18 bound nickel, with dissociation constants from low nanomolar to low micromolar.

blocks.title: Motif scaffolding benchmark: problems solved out of 25

scenes.caption: The 25-problem motif scaffolding benchmark from the RFdiffusion paper: 23 solved, against 15 for hallucination and 19 for inpainting. Scaffolding matters most in practice, since a functional site usually exists already and only needs a protein built around it.

blocks.md:
Where this still breaks, honestly:

- **The representation leaves things out.** Frames carry no side chains, no ligands, no water, no dynamics. A backbone can be designable and still bind nothing, because function lives in chemistry the generator never saw.
- **In silico success is not lab success.** The filters are a predictor grading a generator, and 19 percent binder success means roughly four in five designs that passed every computational filter still failed.
- **Designs are idealised.** Generated structures favour clean, well-packed, mostly idealised topologies similar to what designers already trusted, which is partly why they express and fold well, and partly a limit on novelty.
- **Sampling costs real compute.** Two hundred passes of a structure-prediction-sized network per backbone, times hundreds of backbones, is why FrameFlow's roughly fivefold reduction in sampling steps matters.

blocks.question: Your generator produces 100 backbones and 8 sequences each, and 0 backbones pass the 2 Angstrom filter. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Raise the scRMSD threshold to 5 Angstrom so some designs pass
Fix the backbone generator: a correlated-failure pattern across all 8 sequences points at the geometry, not the sequence design
Sample 100 sequences per backbone instead of 8
Switch AF2 from single-sequence to full MSA mode so predictions improve
blocks.explain: Sequences for one backbone are strongly correlated, so a uniform failure across all 8 is evidence about the backbones. The measured jump from 28 percent at M = 8 to only 40 percent at M = 100 shows how little extra sampling buys. Relaxing the threshold or giving AF2 an MSA hides the problem rather than fixing it.

blocks.question: RFdiffusion starts from pretrained RoseTTAFold weights rather than a fresh network. What does the paper report about that choice?
options: It made no difference once self-conditioning was added
It was needed only for the symmetric oligomer task
Fine-tuning from the pretrained structure prediction weights worked far better than training the same architecture from scratch for the same time
It was done to avoid licensing the PDB training data
blocks.explain: The paper reports that fine-tuning the pretrained RoseTTAFold network substantially outperformed training from untrained weights for an equivalent period. The denoiser's job (map a corrupted structure to a plausible one) overlaps heavily with what a structure predictor already knows. FrameDiff then showed that a from-scratch SE(3) model can also work, so pretraining is helpful rather than strictly necessary.

blocks.question: Which statement about the two-stage pipeline is correct?
options: The backbone generator and the sequence designer are trained jointly, end to end, on experimental binding data
ProteinMPNN generates the backbone and RFdiffusion assigns the sequence
AlphaFold2 is used to generate candidate backbones, and RFdiffusion filters them
The backbone generator never sees a sequence, the sequence designer never changes the backbone, and a structure predictor is the referee between them
blocks.explain: The three models are trained separately and composed at inference. RFdiffusion places frames with no sequence, ProteinMPNN writes a sequence for fixed backbone coordinates, and AF2 or ESMFold judges whether the sequence folds back to the backbone. Nothing in the loop is trained on the assay results.
